title: MySQL (2000) → MongoDB (2010) → PostgreSQL (2020) → PostgreSQL (2030) → PostgreSQL…
author: Franck Pachot
body_html:
I recently saw a slide describing database trends this way: MySQL in the 2000s, MongoDB in the 2010s, and PostgreSQL in the 2020s. The slide aims to explain why PostgreSQL is winning, but I don’t think this framing does it justice. Presenting databases as ten-year waves almost invites an enterprise buyer to ask, “What will be the next box in 2030?” instead of migrating to the latest one. If MySQL was a fashion, then MongoDB was a fashion, and PostgreSQL is today’s fashion, the logical decision is not necessarily to adopt PostgreSQL. It may be to wait for the next fashion. PostgreSQL deserves a stronger explanation.

Just true enough for the narrative

The usual story is compelling because it contains facts. But those facts come from a particular moment in time and are arranged to make every earlier database seem like a historical mistake. That is more dangerous than being completely wrong: it is just true enough.

In this slide, the MySQL story starts with non-standard SQL, permissive behavior, and weak early transactional capabilities. Those limitations were real, but they were not the whole MySQL story. Many developers accessed the database through application frameworks or ORMs and did not care much about SQL-standard differences. And in the LAMP era, simplicity, availability, and easy integration with the application stack mattered more to many developers than SQL-standard purity.

On transactions, InnoDB became a serious engine implementing the ACID properties and undo-based multi-version concurrency control. MySQL also built a strong operational ecosystem around replication, availability, and familiar tooling. Reducing MySQL to its weaknesses in the early 2000s does not explain why so many organizations continued to run it successfully.

The MongoDB narrative is equally simplified: “There was no schema, so the schema moved into the application. There were no joins, so developers had to reimplement the database.” That almost reverses the motivation for the document model. The schema already exists in the application's domain model. Instead of decomposing that model into normalized relations at the storage boundary and reconstructing it through joins, documents allow an aggregate to retain its structure and consistency boundary all the way down to storage. It wasn't about moving the database schema into the application code. It was about pushing the application's data model down into the database.

On durability, WiredTiger is not a toy storage engine either. It uses checkpoints and write-ahead journaling to provide recovery and durability after failures, and MongoDB extends ACID properties to replica sets. This doesn’t make the document model the right answer for every application. It means that choosing it wasn't necessarily a mistake that the next database generation had to correct.

Migration stories contributing to the myth

In 2016, Uber Engineering Switched from Postgres to MySQL presented a detailed critique of PostgreSQL’s storage and replication design. But Uber also acknowledged that much of its analysis reflected its experience with PostgreSQL 9.2 and the requirements of its own architecture. They blamed Postgres's architecture for bloat and write amplification while using default settings, overlooking fillfactor, autovacuum tuning, and transaction timeouts—all of which obviously need to be configured correctly for such a workload.

Changing the database instead of trying to understand it is never a good idea—unless you want another item on your CV. Unfortunately, that article is sometimes cited as evidence against PostgreSQL.

In 2024, “The Great Migration from MongoDB to PostgreSQL” explained why Infisical made the move: its data was highly relational, and the company later reported more efficient joins and a 50% reduction in its database bill. Data is not inherently relational. Relational and document models are two ways to represent data. If Infisical chose a relational model for a document database, it’s no surprise that it didn’t get the best out of it.

That was a data-modeling mistake and a misunderstanding of the original choice of MongoDB. It doesn’t prove that every document database should become relational, just as Uber’s article didn’t prove that PostgreSQL should become MySQL.

The missing argument: who drives the product?

I think PostgreSQL’s more lasting differentiator lies elsewhere: in who drives the product and the direction in which enterprise value is built.

MySQL already used a dual open-source and commercial licensing model before its acquisitions. MySQL AB was acquired by Sun Microsystems in February 2008. Oracle later acquired Sun and became MySQL’s steward in 2010. Oracle continues to offer MySQL under both GPL and commercial licenses. Today, MySQL follows a recognizable commercial product structure: Standard, Enterprise and Cluster editions share the same database lineage, while features such as enterprise backup, TDE, auditing, masking, firewalling and advanced management are associated with commercial editions.

MongoDB followed a different historical path but moved toward a comparable economic model. On October 16, 2018, MongoDB changed Community Server from AGPLv3 to its Server Side Public License. MongoDB explained that the change was intended to prevent cloud providers from offering MongoDB as a service without releasing the software used to provide that service. Today, MongoDB distinguishes its free, source-available Community Edition from Enterprise Advanced, which adds a commercial license, enterprise tooling, operational automation, additional security capabilities, and support.

This was a rational business decision. MongoDB funded the product's development and wanted to capture more of the value it generated. But economically, it put the vendor at the center: the community grows around a product whose direction is ultimately controlled by the company monetizing it.

The traditional enterprise-edition model

This is a familiar model in commercial databases. Oracle Database Standard Edition targets workgroup, departmental, and web applications, while Enterprise Edition serves mission-critical workloads and adds features and separately licensed options. SQL Server presents Enterprise as its high-end datacenter offering, while Standard balances performance, security, and affordability. The editions also differ explicitly in compute, memory, and availability limits. Db2 makes this pattern especially clear: IBM says its editions share the same code base but have different resource limits. Standard is restricted in deployment size, while Community has tighter limits on virtual processors and memory.

In this model, a vendor builds the Enterprise Edition to generate revenue from customers with the largest and most critical deployments. The roadmap, feature priorities, and support model are centered on the Enterprise Edition. The vendor then derives the Standard or Community Edition from it to encourage adoption, build skills, and improve application compatibility across a much larger user base. However, community usage does not drive product strategy.

There’s nothing inherently wrong with this model. It is a rational way for a software vendor to maximize revenue. But it creates an unavoidable economic tension: the community edition must be capable enough to drive adoption, but not so capable that the largest customers no longer need the enterprise offering.

The enterprise product drives the product strategy, while the standard or community offering provides its broad foundation. MySQL and MongoDB followed this path. It's not the only approach: Yugabyte, for example, went the other way, shifting from Enterprise/Community licensing to 100% Open Source in 2019. PostgreSQL never had to make that transition: there is no company-owned PostgreSQL to open up.

PostgreSQL builds enterprise value in the opposite direction

The PostgreSQL ecosystem includes enterprise products, but there is no PostgreSQL "Enterprise Edition.” The project grew out of POSTGRES95 and adopted the PostgreSQL name in 1996. It is released under a permissive license, similar to BSD or MIT, and the PostgreSQL Global Development Group says it intends to keep PostgreSQL free and open source forever. No PostgreSQL product manager decides the roadmap. Development happens publicly through contributions discussed and reviewed by the community. Features reach core when contributors can build consensus around their design, implementation, usefulness, and long-term maintainability. Other ideas may instead live as independently maintained extensions or forks.

Enterprise usage of PostgreSQL therefore grows outward from the community core, with extensions, tools, and forks. Vendors add:

  • managed services and operational automation
  • high availability, disaster recovery, and resilience to failures
  • transparent data encryption and security integrations
  • distributed storage and horizontal scalability
  • observability, backup and lifecycle management
  • specialized extensions and compatibility layers
  • enterprise support and accountability

Some of these additions are open source, while others are proprietary. Some are extensions or forks. Others are cloud services that substantially change the surrounding architecture. The same companies may develop their enterprise managed services while contributing to upstream PostgreSQL. These contributions benefit from enterprise customer feedback, but they are included in core only when they make sense for the PostgreSQL community: when they benefit the broader community, introduce no unacceptable side effects for other use cases, and, most importantly, can be supported and maintained independently of the commercial vendor that contributed them.

The key point is the direction in which value is created: the enterprise offering is built on community PostgreSQL, rather than PostgreSQL serving as the free tier of an enterprise product. With MySQL and MongoDB, the vendor sits at the center, and the community surrounds its product. With PostgreSQL, the community project sits at the center and vendors surround it with their products. The commercial incentives haven't disappeared. They moved outside the core. PostgreSQL’s evolution remains driven by its community.

That's why I don't see PostgreSQL as simply the next box in the ten-year cycle. It may be what breaks the cycle.

So what comes after PostgreSQL?

PostgreSQL will not remain popular because it is technically perfect. It isn’t. But it's good enough. It will remain relevant if its ecosystem can absorb the requirements that once created a new database category: documents, vectors, geospatial data, distributed SQL, time series, analytics, horizontal scaling, serverless operations, and whatever comes next. Some of those capabilities will enter the core. Some will remain extensions. Some will be implemented by managed services or forks. But they can all evolve around a common core whose direction is not controlled by any one vendor's revenue model.

That is why the 2030 box may still say PostgreSQL. Not because database innovation has stopped. Not because MySQL and MongoDB were mistakes. And not because PostgreSQL happened to win the fashion cycle of the 2020s. It may still say PostgreSQL because a trend needs to be replaced, while an underlying foundation can keep growing to support what comes next.

So I would not sell PostgreSQL by making other databases look stupid. They are not. I would sell it by explaining why tomorrow’s database vendors may still choose to build around an upstream they do not own.
